client: I've been really stressed out lately because my final exams are coming up next month and I just feel like I'm already behind. I had this whole study schedule planned out, but I keep falling behind on it, and now every time I think about the exams I get this tight feeling in my chest. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help me actually catch up or make the anxiety go away.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of weight right now — that tight feeling in your chest and the racing thoughts about falling behind tell me this stress is very real, and I notice even in the way you're speaking there's a kind of quiet urgency, like you're holding a lot in. It's also completely understandable to feel skeptical about whether talking helps, but that doubt itself is worth exploring — because the belief that you're "already too far behind to recover" might be adding to your anxiety more than the actual gap in your study schedule. Together, we can start to untangle what's a real obstacle versus what's your mind catastrophizing under pressure, and find small, concrete steps that can help you feel more in control.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess that makes sense, that maybe I'm making it feel worse than it actually is, but it's hard to really believe that when I look at my notes and see how much I haven't covered yet. Like, it doesn't feel like catastrophizing when the evidence is right there in front of me, you know? I'm just not sure how separating "real" from "catastrophizing" is supposed to help me actually get through the material faster.
therapist: You're raising a really fair point, and I can hear in your voice — soft but carrying a kind of quiet heaviness — that this isn't just overthinking for you, it feels grounded in real evidence. You're right that the uncovered material is real, but here's the CBT distinction worth considering: the facts say "there's material left to study," while the catastrophizing adds "and therefore I'm going to fail, I can't handle this, it's hopeless" — and that second layer is what creates the chest tightness and makes it harder to actually sit down and study. Separating them doesn't make the work disappear, but it can free up the mental energy that's currently being consumed by dread, so you can actually use it to move forward.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Okay, I can kind of see the difference you're drawing there, and I think I do tell myself things like "I'm definitely going to fail" even when I don't know that for sure. But the thing is, even when I try to push those thoughts away, they just come back, especially late at night when I'm trying to sleep and everything feels so much bigger and darker. I'm not sure I know how to actually separate those layers in the moment when the anxiety is already spiking.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly, almost carefully — makes me think part of you is genuinely trying to work through this even as it feels overwhelming, and that matters. You've actually just done something really important by noticing the thought "I'm definitely going to fail" is a prediction, not a fact — and in CBT, we don't try to push those thoughts away (which, as you've noticed, tends to make them louder), but instead practice catching them and gently asking "what's the actual evidence for and against this?" The late-night spiral is especially common because your mind is tired and has no distractions, so one practical tool is keeping a small notepad by your bed to write the thought down and one piece of counter-evidence, which externalizes it just enough to reduce its grip.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: The notepad idea sounds simple enough, but I honestly worry that in the moment I'll just write down the thought and then not be able to come up with any counter-evidence because my brain is already in that dark place. Like, when it's 2am and I'm convinced I'm going to fail, it genuinely feels like there's no evidence on the other side, even if logically I know I've passed exams before. I guess I'm just not sure I trust myself to do it right, especially when I'm already that anxious.
therapist: The softness in your voice, combined with what you just shared, tells me this worry runs pretty deep — and I want to gently point out that you actually just provided your own counter-evidence in the same breath: "I know I've passed exams before." That's not nothing, and the fact that it feels unconvincing at 2am doesn't make it less true — it just means anxiety is a very loud filter that distorts how much weight we give to real evidence. So for the notepad, we can actually make it easier by pre-writing your counter-evidence *now*, while you're calmer, so that late-night version of you doesn't have to generate it from scratch — just read what your clearer-headed self already knew was true.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That actually does make a weird kind of sense, like having a note from a calmer version of myself waiting there. But I'm a little worried that when I'm in that 2am spiral, I'll just read it and think "yeah but that was before, this time is different" and dismiss it completely. I guess I'm just not sure how to stop my anxious brain from arguing against even the evidence I've already prepared.
therapist: There's something in your voice right now — a kind of tense alertness, like you're bracing for the ways this might not work — and that actually makes a lot of sense given how many times anxiety has talked you out of things that seemed reasonable. What you're describing is a classic feature of anxious thinking called "yes, but" reasoning, where the mind keeps moving the goalposts, and the important thing to know is that you don't have to *win* that argument at 2am — the goal of the note isn't to silence anxiety completely, but just to create enough of a pause to stop the spiral from accelerating. So we can even write that into the note itself: something like "I know part of me will say 'this time is different' — that's just what anxiety does, and I don't have to believe it."
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That actually catches me a little off guard, because I hadn't thought about building the "yes, but" response into the note itself. I think part of me is still skeptical that reading a piece of paper is going to feel like enough when the anxiety is really bad, but I also realize I've never actually tried anything like this before, so maybe I'm just assuming it won't work. I guess I'm willing to try writing the note, though I'm still nervous about whether I'll even remember to reach for it in that moment instead of just lying there spiraling.
therapist: There's something meaningful in the way you just said that — softly, almost tentatively, like a small door opening — and I want to reflect back what I heard: you caught yourself assuming it won't work before you've even tried, and that kind of self-awareness is actually a really important CBT skill in itself. The worry about remembering to reach for the note is real, so we can make it even easier by placing it somewhere unavoidable — like on your phone screen or on your pillow before bed — so it's already in your hand before the spiral fully takes hold. You don't have to feel confident it will work to try it once, and one real experience will tell you far more than any amount of predicting.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Putting it on my pillow actually feels doable in a way that some of the other stuff hasn't, because it removes the part where I have to remember to do something when I'm already overwhelmed. I think my bigger fear now is less about the note and more about what happens if I try it and it doesn't help, because then I'll feel like even this small thing failed and that might make the whole spiral worse. But I hear what you're saying about one real experience being worth more than predicting, so I guess I can at least try it before writing it off.
therapist: There's something genuinely hopeful in your voice right now — still soft and a little cautious, but with a quality that feels different from earlier, like you're standing just a little closer to trying. I want to gently name what you just did though: you identified a new fear — "what if even this small thing fails" — which is anxiety already preparing its next defense before you've even attempted anything, and that pattern itself is worth noticing rather than believing. If the note doesn't help perfectly the first time, that's not proof you're beyond help — it's just information we use to adjust, and one imperfect attempt is still more than anxiety wants you to risk.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: It's a little unsettling to realize how quickly my brain jumped to the next worst-case scenario before I'd even tried the first thing, like anxiety is always one step ahead of me. I think what you said about it being "information to adjust" rather than proof of failure is actually helpful, because I've always treated any setback as confirmation that I'm doomed, especially with exams. I'm still nervous, but I think I can write the note tonight and put it on my pillow, even if part of me is already bracing for it not to work perfectly.
therapist: The quickness and energy in your voice right now actually mirrors exactly what you're describing — your mind moving fast, a little unsettled, but also genuinely engaged in a way that feels different from where we started. What you just said is a real breakthrough: you've named the pattern where setbacks become "proof of doom," and simply seeing that pattern clearly is what starts to loosen its grip over time. Writing that note tonight — nervousness and all — is exactly the right next step, and the fact that part of you is already bracing for imperfection doesn't disqualify you from trying; it just means you're human, and you're doing it anyway.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think what's sticking with me most is that phrase "you're doing it anyway," because I don't usually give myself credit for trying something even when I'm scared, I just focus on whether it worked or not. It's a small shift but it feels like it might actually matter for how I approach the exams too, not just the note. I'm still anxious about everything, but I feel a little less like I'm completely alone with it right now.
therapist: There's a warmth and openness in your voice right now that feels genuinely different from how you sounded at the start of our conversation, and I think that shift reflects something real that happened here today. What you've just identified — that you deserve credit for trying, not just for succeeding — is actually one of the most important cognitive shifts in CBT, because it moves you from measuring your worth by outcomes you can't fully control to recognizing the courage in the effort itself. You're not alone with this, and you're already doing the thing you said you weren't sure you could do: sitting with the anxiety and moving forward anyway.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Hearing you say that I'm already doing it actually makes me feel a bit emotional, which is kind of unexpected because I came in here pretty convinced this wouldn't help much. I think I've spent so long grading myself on whether I pass or fail the exam that I forgot there's a whole process happening before that, and maybe that process counts for something. I'm going to write the note tonight, and I guess I'll try to remember that trying counts, even if part of me is still waiting for it to go wrong.
therapist: The emotion in your voice right now — quick, a little breathless, pitched high like something just cracked open — tells me this landed somewhere deep and real, and it makes complete sense that it's unexpected, because you came in with your guard up and something genuinely shifted anyway. What you just said about forgetting the process is profound: you've been so focused on the verdict that you've been invisible to yourself through all the hard, quiet work of trying. Carry that with you tonight when you write the note — that the version of you who showed up here today, skeptical and scared and willing anyway, is already someone worth being proud of.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
